person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: fear of COVID-19 as a measurable construct in the general Iranian population
span.quote: One of the reasons that current treatment on COVID-19 pays little attention to the fear of COVID-19 is the lack of an appropriate psychometric instrument. Therefore, developing a brief and valid instrument to capture an individual’s fear of COVID-19 is both timely and important.

span.label: whether a brief self-report instrument can measure fear of COVID-19 reliably and validly
span.quote: One of the reasons that current treatment on COVID-19 pays little attention to the fear of COVID-19 is the lack of an appropriate psychometric instrument. Therefore, developing a brief and valid instrument to capture an individual’s fear of COVID-19 is both timely and important.

span.label: the seven-item Fear of COVID-19 Scale, with classical test theory and Rasch psychometrics on 717 participants
span.quote: In conclusion, this study demonstrated that the Fear of COVID-19 Scale is a seven-item unidimensional scale with robust psychometric properties. Moreover, total scores on the FCV-19S are comparable across both genders and all ages which suggest that it is a good psychometric instrument to be used in assessing and allaying fears of COVID-19 among individuals.

span.label: method
span.quote: The present study presented the development of a new scale, the Fear of COVID-19 Scale (FC-19S). Findings demonstrated that the FCV-19S has a stable unidimensional structure with robust psychometric properties.

span.label: fear as a distinguishing feature of infectious disease, tied to transmission rate and mortality
span.quote: One characteristic nature of infectious disease compared with other conditions is fear. Fear is directly associated with its transmission rate and medium (rapidly and invisibly) as well as its morbidity and mortality.

span.label: item generation from a literature review, two expert panels, a pilot, then item-total correlation, EFA and Rasch analysis
span.term: item generation from a literature review, two expert panels, a pilot, then item-total correlation, EFA and Rasch analysis
span.quote: First, an extensive literature review was conducted to assess all general scales on fear. Thirty measures on fear were identified that assess fear on different populations and diseases (available on request from the corresponding authors). Relevant and possible items were pooled by two researchers (i.e., the third and last authors). After removing those items with similar content or expressions, 28 items were retained for further evaluation. Second, an expert panel (comprising a psychologist, virologist, health psychologist, psychiatrist, general physician, and nurse) evaluated the 28 items, and 11 items were deleted based on the suggestion from the expert panel. Third, the retained 17 items were sent out to a different expert panel (comprising a health education specialist, pulmonologist, social psychologist, and sociologist in Iran) to review. Seven items were further omitted based on the comments from the second expert panel.

span.label: the construct is not defined in advance and then measured; it is whatever remains after a literature pool is cut by two expert panels and then by an item-total correlation threshold
span.quote: First, an extensive literature review was conducted to assess all general scales on fear. span.label: the paper treats fear as a feature of infectious disease itself, tied to transmission rate and medium as well as morbidity and mortality, rather than as a reaction in individuals only
span.quote: One characteristic nature of infectious disease compared with other conditions is fear. Fear is directly associated with its transmission rate and medium (rapidly and invisibly) as well as its morbidity and mortality.

span.label: no formal diagnoses were obtained, so the scale's sensitivity and specificity cannot be examined
span.quote: First, the studied participants were from the general Iranian population and no formal diagnoses on mood disorders were obtained (e.g., anxiety). Therefore, the sensitivity and specificity of the scale cannot be examined.

span.label: self-report cannot exclude responses shaped by social desirability, and fear is subjective
span.quote: Second, although fear is subjective and has shortcomings when trying to assess it objectively, the nature of the self-report cannot exclude the possibility that respondents provided responses affected by social desirability factors.

span.label: convenience sampling weakens generalisability
span.quote: Third, convenience sampling weakens the generalizability of the findings in the present study.

span.label: the single-factor structure rests on EFA and Rasch analysis and still needs confirmatory factor analysis
span.quote: Finally, the single-factor structure of the scale was based on EFA and Rasch analysis; consequently, further verification, such as using confirmatory factor analysis, on its factor structure is needed.

span.label: the item pool itself, taken from thirty existing fear scales built for other populations and diseases
span.quote: First, an extensive literature review was conducted to assess all general scales on fear. span.label: measurement invariance across gender and age, tested by differential item functioning
span.note: eliminates: a scale that measures a different thing in men and women, or in the young and the old, being used to compare them · outcome: held
span.quote: All factor loadings from the retained seven items were significant and strong (0.66 to 0.74). Their properties tested using Rasch analysis were satisfactory: infit MnSq values were between 0.80 and 1.26; outfit MnSq values were between 0.84 and 1.25. No substantial DIF was found across gender and age (Table 2).

span.label: whether pilot participants understood the item wording, checked by rating and by telephone cognitive interview
span.note: eliminates: a factor structure fitted to responses given to items the respondents read differently from the way the authors meant them · outcome: held
span.quote: Finally, the 10-item scale was piloted on 46 individuals (26 males and 20 females, mean age 39.63 years, number of years in education = 9.38 years) to obtain initial assessment of the scale. A four-point Likert scale was used to test whether the individuals understand the item descriptions. The results showed that all respondents fully understood the item descriptions (mean 3.81, SD = 1.04).

span.label: concurrent validity against two established scales, the HADS and the PVDS
span.note: eliminates: a new fear scale that is a relabelling of the anxiety and depression instruments already in use · outcome: held
span.quote: There were significant positive correlations between fear of COVID-19 and (i) depression (r = 0.425, p < 0.001), (ii) anxiety (r = 0.511, p < 0.001), (iii) perceived infectability (r = 0.483, p < 0.001), and (iv) germ aversion (r = 0.459, p < 0.001).

span.label: the test-retest reliability the abstract reports as ICC = .72
span.note: eliminates: an unstable instrument - a scale that gives a different answer on a second administration cannot support the claims built on it · outcome: held
span.quote: More specifically, reliability values such as internal consistency (α = .82) and test–retest reliability (ICC = .72) were acceptable.

span.label: corrected item-total correlation
span.quote: According to the corrected inter-item correlation, three items with low corrected item-total correlations were deleted (i.e., Item 3, − 0.06; Item 4, − 0.03; Item 5 − 0.05). The remaining seven items in the scale all had acceptable corrected item-total correlation (0.47 to 0.56) and were used for following psychometric testing (Table 1).

span.label: internal consistency
span.quote: From CTT analysis, the internal consistency was good (α = .82), composite reliability (0.88) and AVE (0.51) were acceptable, and standard error of measurement was low (1.89).

span.label: concurrent validity
span.quote: Analyses on psychometric properties included CTT analysis and Rasch model analysis. CTT analysis included internal consistency, test-retest reliability, corrected item-total correlation, average variance extracted (AVE), composite reliability, standard error of measurement, concurrent validity, and exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Rasch model analysis included infit and outfit mean square (MnSq) for each item, item and person separation reliability, and item and person separation index. Also, differential item functioning (DIF) based on Rasch analysis was used to test the measurement invariance across gender and age (Wu et al.).
